summary: Western Sahara is a disputed territory in northwestern Africa, listed by the United Nations as a Non-Self-Governing Territory; most of it is controlled by Morocco, while the east is controlled by the Polisario Front, which has proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: The Almoravid movement, which arose in the 11th century in this western part of the Sahara, was launched by the Sanhaja Berber tribes and unified North Africa and the southern Iberian Peninsula under Maliki Sunni Islam. From the 13th to the 17th century the Arab Beni Hassan tribes gradually moved south, further blending Islam and Arab culture into the nomadic society of the Sahrawis. Sufi orders and families of religious scholars hold high standing in tribal society, so Islam is the faith of almost the entire Sahrawi population.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In 1884 Spain declared a protectorate over this coast and established Spanish Sahara, and as a result Catholic churches appeared in cities such as Laayoune and Dakhla. After Spain withdrew in 1975 most Europeans left with it, and today only scattered expatriates and churches remain, so Christians are very few.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: Followers of other faiths are mainly foreign personnel and staff of the United Nations peacekeeping mission (the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, established in 1991); very few have settled in the area long term.

religion.background: Berber nomadic peoples were active in Western Sahara before the Middle Ages, and the Almoravid movement arose from here in the 11th century, making Islam the mainstream across all of northwestern Africa. The subsequent arrival of Arab tribes merged with the Berbers, forming a Sahrawi society that follows Sunni Islam and values tribal and religious-scholar traditions. During Spanish colonization from 1884 to 1975, Catholicism existed only in the colonial towns. After 1975, with Morocco controlling most of the area, Islam remains the only major religion there.

language.official: In the area controlled by Morocco, Arabic and Berber are the official languages; the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic has Arabic as its official language and Spanish as a second language.

ranking.name: Hassaniya Arabic
ranking.description: Hassaniya Arabic takes its name from the Beni Hassan tribes who moved south from the Arabian Peninsula through North Africa in the 13th–17th centuries. After the “Char Bouba War” of the 17th century (1644–1674), the Arab tribes gained the upper hand, and the nomads who had originally spoken Berber gradually switched to Hassaniya. It is the mother tongue of the Sahrawis, is also spoken in Mauritania, and is likewise used in the refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria.

ranking.name: Moroccan Arabic
ranking.description: After Spain withdrew in 1975 and Morocco launched the “Green March” and took over, the Moroccan government encouraged its own residents to move to cities such as Laayoune and provided subsidies, so Moroccan Arabic (Darija) became widespread in the cities, and administration and education also operate under the Moroccan system, bringing its speakers close to half.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: During Spanish colonization from 1884 to 1975, Spanish was the language of administration and schools, and many older Sahrawis can use it. The Polisario Front, which fights for independence, still keeps Spanish as a second language, and many students in the refugee camps have also studied in Cuba and Spain, but there are few speakers in the Moroccan-controlled area.

language.history: The early inhabitants of Western Sahara spoke Berber; after the Arab Beni Hassan tribes moved south from the 13th century, Hassaniya Arabic gradually replaced Berber and became the common language of the Sahrawis, though it kept quite a few Berber words. Spanish colonization in 1884 brought Spanish. After 1975 Morocco controlled about two-thirds of the land, and large-scale immigration increased the influence of Moroccan Arabic and French, while the Sahrawis in the camps in Algeria maintain the use of both Hassaniya and Spanish.

ranking.name: Mint tea
ranking.description: Chinese green tea is brewed with plenty of fresh mint and sugar, poured from a height into small glasses to produce foam, and usually three glasses are drunk in a sitting.
ranking.history: Tea reached Moroccan ports through British merchants in the 18th–19th centuries, and during the Crimean War of the 1850s British merchants turned to dumping tea in North Africa, and the habit of drinking tea spread to the Sahara with the caravans. The Sahrawi tea ceremony calls for brewing slowly in three rounds, and a saying goes, “The first glass is bitter like life, the second sweet like love, the third gentle like death.” Making and serving tea is the central etiquette of hospitality and conversation and often lasts for hours in the tent.

ranking.name: Couscous
ranking.description: Coarse wheat or barley flour is steamed into loose small grains and topped with a broth stewed from lamb, camel meat or vegetables; it is a festive staple of the Sahara region.
ranking.history: Couscous originated with the Berbers of North Africa, was widely eaten by the Middle Ages at the latest, and spread to the Sahara region with trade and tribal migration. In the arid Western Sahara it is often made with drought-tolerant barley and served with the camel or goat meat raised by nomads. It is the family feast after Friday prayers and on religious holidays, and also an important dish for entertaining honored guests.

ranking.name: Méchoui (whole roast lamb)
ranking.description: A whole sheep is marinated with butter and spices and roasted slowly over charcoal or in a pit until the meat is tender, torn off by hand and dipped in cumin and salt to eat.
ranking.history: Whole roast lamb is the most ceremonious hospitality dish of the nomadic peoples of North Africa and the Sahara, and for the Sahrawis, who live by herding, slaughtering a whole sheep for guests expresses the highest respect. It often appears at weddings, Eid al-Adha and tribal gatherings, with guests sitting on carpets and eating by hand. After France colonized North Africa, the word “méchoui” also entered France with returning settlers.

ranking.name: Tagine
ranking.description: Meat, vegetables, olives, preserved lemon and spices are slow-cooked in a clay pot with a conical lid, concentrating the broth and tenderizing the meat.
ranking.history: The tagine originated with the Berbers of North Africa, and the conical lid lets steam condense and flow back, which is especially useful in water-scarce desert regions, as food can be stewed with only a little water. After Morocco took over Western Sahara in 1975, the large number of Moroccan residents who moved in made tagine dishes even more common in the local cities. It is the centerpiece of everyday family dinners, and a version with Saharan character can also be made with camel meat.

ranking.name: Camel milk
ranking.description: The milk of the camels raised by Saharan nomads, slightly salty and sour in taste and rich in nutrients, can be drunk as is, or fermented or diluted with water into a beverage.
ranking.history: For generations the Sahrawis have lived in the desert following water and pasture by raising camels; camel milk is nutritious and supplies fluid in the heat, making it one of the most important foods of nomadic life, and in times of food shortage it can even serve as the only source of food. Traditionally it is also used to welcome guests who have come from afar, symbolizing generosity and hospitality. Even though most people have now settled in cities, camel milk is still regarded as a symbol of Sahrawi identity and nomadic tradition.
